claim: The FBI's 2006 Moussaoui-trial exhibit P200054 documents the phone calls from UA Flight 93. The FBI's official tally of UA93 calls was '35 air phone calls and two cell phone calls' — 13 passengers and crew using GTE Airfones built into seat-backs in the last nine rows of the plane, and just two cell-phone calls, both placed at 9:58 a.m. by CeeCee Lyles and Edward Felt during the plane's final low-altitude descent (UA93 had descended to roughly 5,000 feet by the 9:58 mark). The claim that the Flight 93 phone calls were fabricated rests on the theory that cell-phone calls at altitude were technically impossible; checked against P200054, the record cuts the other way. The specific argument that 'CeCe's call took place at 9:47, which means she would have been at 20,000 feet' confuses two separate Lyles calls: the 9:47 a.m. call that went to her husband Lorne Lyles' answering machine was an Airfone call, while her 9:58 a.m. cell-phone call to a residential number happened during descent at ~5,000 feet. The separate complaint about audio clarity ('no background noise') applies to Airfone audio, which is a wired in-flight handset and would not pick up cabin/engine background the way a cell-phone mic at altitude would. The frequently-cited quote from Theodore Olson — that 'the government has [an] inherent right' / 'legitimate reasons to give out false information' — is real. Olson, then Solicitor General, said it at oral argument in Christopher v. Harbury, 536 U.S. 403 (argued March 18, 2002, decided June 20, 2002), a case brought by Jennifer Harbury alleging State Department officials deceived her while her husband was being tortured and killed by CIA-paid Guatemalan army officers. The Supreme Court ruled unanimously against Harbury on access-to-courts grounds, dismissing the constitutional claim without resolving the underlying right-to-lie question.

sources.quote: There are lots of different situations when the government has legitimate reasons to give out false information

notes: The reel's strongest hook is the Olson quote, which is verbatim and on the record. The weakest is the timeline conflation between CeeCee Lyles' 9:47 a.m. Airfone voicemail and her 9:58 a.m. cell-phone call — the same conflation appears in most of the 'cell phones don't work at 20,000 feet' truther material. The FBI's own count (35 Airfone + 2 cell) is the durable factual frame; the Lyles audio 'too clean' complaint dissolves once the call is identified as an in-flight Airfone rather than a cell connection. Theodore Olson's wife Barbara Olson, on AA77, was reported by Olson initially as a cell-phone call; FBI exhibits in the Moussaoui trial later listed AA77's call-records as zero connected cell calls and the Barbara Olson call as a possibly unconnected Airfone attempt — this is a separate thread and warrants its own record if pursued.
